LESSON 102 OF 106·Cyber Security in the Real World

Building a Home and Small-Business Security Program

A security programme a two-person organisation can actually run: what to do in the right order, which habits do the most work, and what not to buy first.

Applied Foundation14 min
Why this matters

Most of the serious attacks on small organisations and home setups are opportunistic rather than targeted. A small number of habits removes most of that exposure, and the habits are not expensive.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Small environments have the same weaknesses as large ones and none of the defences, so defaults are the real risk.
  • Automatic updates on everything reachable from the internet is the single highest-value action.
  • Administrative separation matters even at home, because it stops a compromised everyday account reaching everything.
  • Backups on a separate medium, tested occasionally, are what distinguish a bad day from a bad month.
  • The people who run small environments are also the people who must respond to an incident, which is a capacity problem.

The background

  • Home and small business computing was consumer-grade and assumed the router was the boundary.
  • Cloud services moved most of the estate off-premises, which removed the boundary but added account risk.
  • Ransomware shifted from targeting organisations to targeting whoever is reachable, including home machines.
  • Remote work made home networks business networks, which removed the distinction entirely.

Real-world examples

  • An unpatched router or camera is compromised and used to reach devices inside, which is routine and automated.
  • A reused password on a service that holds your email is the most valuable credential you own.
  • A backup on the same device as the original protects against nothing except accidental deletion.

What to look for

  • Check what is reachable from the internet, including remote access tools you may have installed and forgotten.
  • Check whether updates are automatic on the router, cameras, laptops and phones.
  • Check whether the account that manages everything is separate from the everyday account.
  • Check whether backups are off the device and whether you have ever restored one.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

NCSC — 10 Steps to Cyber Security

Walking a national authority's ten-step baseline in order and writing, for each step, what it would mean for a very small organisation and who would own it

Open NCSC resource ↗

CISA — Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals

Selecting a first group of voluntary high-impact practices and turning each one into a named, owned action for a small organisation

Open CISA resource ↗

Key takeaways

  • Turn on automatic updates everywhere, and prioritise the devices that face the internet.
  • Use a password manager and a separate, generated password for every account, with multi-factor on email first.
  • Do not expose remote access to anything; use a brokered service that does not require inbound connections.
  • Keep two backups, one of them offline, and test a restore once a year.
  • Write down what to do first if something goes wrong, so you are not deciding it while panicking.
